study.title: Aptamer-functionalized EGCG nanocarrier for neutrophil-targeted AKBA delivery promotes anxiety-related fracture healing

cover.headline: Stress-driven anxiety might interfere with bone repair by **triggering a damaging immune response** at breaks.

slides.title: If this pattern holds in people, it could explain why anxious patients heal more slowly after a break.
slides.body:
Clinicians have long observed that anxious patients tend to have worse fracture outcomes. This study offers a possible mechanism: chronic stress appears linked to the expansion of a specific neutrophil type.

If the same pathway exists in humans, it could open routes to therapies that target the immune response rather than just managing pain.

slides.title: In anxious mice with broken femurs, a subset of neutrophils expanded and blocked the bone cells needed for healing.
slides.body:
The researchers used chronic restraint stress to model anxiety in mice, then induced femoral fractures. Stressed mice showed higher numbers of TGFβ1+CCR5+ neutrophils in bone marrow.

A targeted nanocarrier delivering AKBA reduced this neutrophil population and sped up fracture repair compared to free drug.

stat.label: neutrophil marker linked to impaired healing

slides.title: The assumption is that bone healing is mainly about mechanical stability and nutrient supply, not immune cells.
slides.body:
Most fracture care focuses on alignment, casting, and supporting calcium intake. But this work shows neutrophils can form a feedback loop with stem cells that stalls bone formation.

The nanocarrier was designed to home in on neutrophils at the fracture site, solving problems with AKBA's poor solubility.

caveats: This study found a pattern, not a cause. Something else could explain the link between stress and impaired healing.
This was done in mice, not humans. Most findings in mice do not carry over to people, and the immune systems differ substantially.

source.abstract: Anxiety is clinically associated with impaired fracture healing, but the underlying immunological mechanism remains unclear, and no targeted therapy is available. In a mouse model of chronic restraint stress (CRS)-induced anxiety with femoral fracture, we observed expansion of TGFβ1+CCR5+ double-positive neutrophils in the bone marrow. These neutrophils inhibited osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) via TGFβ1 secretion, while BMSC-derived CCL5 reciprocally promoted neutrophil activation, forming a detrimental feedback that disrupted fracture repair. Mechanistically, CRS activated the NF-κB-CCR5 axis to upregulate CCR5 and sustain this neutrophil subset. We found that acetyl-11-keto-β-boswellic acid (AKBA) directly bound YAP1, relieved YAP1-mediated suppression of ubiquitin-specific peptidase 31 (USP31), and consequently inhibited NF-κB phosphorylation and CCR5 expression, reducing the pathogenic neutrophil population and restoring BMSCs' osteogenic function. In order to overcome the problems of poor solubility, low bioavailability and tissue non-selectivity of AKBA, we developed a NIMP-R14 aptamer-modified epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG)-coated nanocarrier (AKBA@E-N), which can achieve enhanced uptake and local retention of neutrophils in the acidic microenvironment of the fracture site. In vivo, AKBA@E-N significantly accelerated fracture healing compared with free AKBA. This study reveals a neutrophil-mediated mechanism linking stress to impaired bone repair and provides a targeted nanotherapeutic strategy.
